gist: Asked which trade eats the most, the answer names bricklayers because the German verb for plastering a house also means wolfing food down.

wordplay.explanation: German 'verputzen' means both to plaster a wall and, colloquially, to devour food.

en.note: Needs an English trade verb meaning both building work and eating a lot, e.g. 'put away'.

gist: A truck too tall for a low bridge worries the passenger, but the driver only cares whether police are around to see it.

en.note: Units can stay in meters or switch to feet.

driver leaning out of car window, flirty smile

wordplay.explanation: German 'abgefahren' means both worn down (tires) and slang 'awesome, wild'.

ru.note: Find a tire-condition word that can be misheard as praise.

en.note: Find a tire-condition word that sounds like a compliment, e.g. 'your tires are really bald... well, your lights are hot'.

gist: Red Riding Hood asks the wolf the classic 'why such big eyes' question, but he is wide-eyed only because she caught him relieving himself behind a tree.

big grey wolf, crouching, bulging angry eyes

gist: A mother explains black humor by telling her child to give an armless man a gift to open, and when the child objects that he is blind, she says that is black humor.

gist: You cannot pick up a dropped clock because you lack the rights, a pun merging the German words for copyright and lifting a clock.

gist: Baby beavers, who gnaw wood, want 'table sticks' for lunch, a one-letter twist on fish sticks.

en.note: Needs an English food pun with wood, e.g. a twist on 'fish sticks'.

gist: A Chuck Norris fact: his car runs neither on gas nor electricity but out of respect for him.

gist: Photos taken during a hospital stay are called emergency shots, because the German word for emergency room also means emergency pictures.

en.note: Rework around 'shots' or 'ER' double meaning.

gist: Grandpa came back from the war with one leg, and the twist is that it was an extra leg belonging to someone else.

characters.looks: tough bearded man, cowboy hat, smug poker face

English race start command 'On your marks'

gist: Copper wire is said to be made by throwing a cent between two stingy people who stretch it fighting over it.

wordplay.explanation: 'Punkte' means both loyalty points and spots (a Dalmatian's dots).

gist: An employee calls to say he will be late on Monday, and when asked when he will arrive answers Tuesday.

characters.looks: sleepy man in pajamas, phone at ear
boss in suit and tie at a desk, phone

gist: A doctor explains suppositories in ever cruder terms until he says the common insult 'shove it up your ass', which the patient takes as an insult instead of the instruction.

dad in armchair, newspaper, wry smile
bearded old man in white robe, clouds

en.note: Craftsmen can be contractors.

gist: Two lunatics at a closed railway crossing conclude a train just passed because they can still see its tracks, taking the rails for traces.

wild-haired man in robe, amazed face

small cannibal kid with a lunchbox

wordplay.explanation: 'Leberwurstbrot' (liverwurst sandwich) becomes 'Lehrerwurstbrot' (teacher-sausage sandwich).

gist: A patient on a gurney protests he is not dead yet as he is wheeled to the morgue, and the doctor replies they are not there yet either.

gist: What hangs on jungle trees is 'vacation', because the German word splits into ancient-forest foliage.

big shaggy dog passing by

gist: A scientist eats a 'scientifically proven' roll for breakfast, the German word for proven also meaning a topped sandwich.
